# Overview
This report summarises neuropsychological test results for a single patient/client.
In its current iteration, *WarpScore* imports patient data; generates a custom
normative dataset based on available patient descriptives (age and education); 
and then computes a test of deficit for the individual patient score relative 
to the data from the normative sample.

*WarpScore* employs the _R_ package [singcar](https://github.com/jorittmo/singcar)
to implement the Baysian test of deficit (BTD) described in [Crawford & Garthwaite (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1080/02643290701290146). In brief, this method appropriately treats means and standard deviations derived from normative samples
as _statistics_. This is in contrast to the common and flawed clinical neuropsychology practice of using _z_-score-based differences, treating normative sample means and standard deviations as _parameters_ and thereby ignoring normative sample sizes (which tend to be small/moderate). Note that, as the normative sample size approaches infinity, the percentile interval of the Bayesian estimate becomes vanishingly small and the results from the BTD and _z_-score methods converge. 

Finally, because BTD uses Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimation, some variation (*i.e.* simulation variance) is expected in the results. (So if the same input data is used to repeatedly generate multiple reports, the estimated probabilities and percentile intervals will fluctuate.)

See the **Appendix** for further details related to *WarpScore* and the attendant limitations and licensing.

## How to read this report
1. Verify that patien/client data is correct
2. Review the generated normative dataset and confirm that it appears as expected
3. Examine and interpret the **Results** (shown below in graphical and tabulated formats)

Note that the table of contents on the left of the report can be used to navigate through the report sections.

## Graph
```{r WarpScore_OutputGraph, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=15, fig.height=10}

```
Posterior probability point-estimates (and associated 95% percentile intervals) corresponding to the percentage of the population that would be expected to obtain a worse score than the patient. There is a 95% probability that the patient's true discrepancy value lies within the specified interval. Numbers above each bar are values of point-estimates rounded up to whole number (_i.e._ minimum possible value is 1). Colour gradations (ROYGBIV) correspond to the interpretive ranges and labels adopted by the [American Academy of Clinical Neuropsychology consensus conference statement on uniform labeling of performance test scores](https://doi.org/10.1080/13854046.2020.1722244).

## Table
Bayesian _t_-distribution and classic (normal-distribution) estimates of score prevalence. Lower posterior probability estimates indicate worse performance (_e.g._ slower or less accurate responses) or worse symptom burden (_e.g._ higher fatigue/stress, lower environmental rewards).
```{r WarpScore_OutputTable, echo=F, message=T}

```
df = degrees of freedom; p.value = posterior probability point-estimate (based on _t_-distribution); L.PI = 2.5^th^ percentile of the posterior distribution; H.PI = 97.5^th^ percentile of the posterior distribution; zscore = classic _z_-score; PR = percentile rank (based on normal distribution, i.e. _z_-score);
Input = patient/client and control/normative parameters used in the Bayesian test of deficit (BTD).
